sections.section_title: Assessment of a woman in labour

blocks.text: **“A 24-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks presents with painful uterine contractions. Assess her.”**
**“A woman in labour has been admitted to the labour ward. Perform an assessment.”**

items.text: What stage of labour is she in?
How frequent and strong are contractions?
Is the fetus alive and well?
What is the fetal heart rate?
Is there evidence of fetal compromise?

blocks.text: A good candidate briefly establishes the relevant history.
“Have they become stronger or more frequent?”
“Contractions are occurring every 3 minutes and lasting approximately 50 seconds.”
“Have you noticed any blood-stained mucus or show?”
A show may occur as the cervix begins to change in labour.
But significant vaginal bleeding is **not simply a normal show** and requires assessment.
“Have you felt the baby moving normally?”
Reduced fetal movements require appropriate fetal assessment.
Do not assume that hearing a fetal heart rate automatically makes reduced fetal movements unimportant.
Where clinically indicated, particularly if the mother is unwell or breathless.
Place your hand gently over the fundus.
How many contractions occur in 10 minutes?
How long does each contraction last?
“There are four contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting approximately 50 seconds and of moderate-to-strong intensity.”
At term, a transverse lie is clinically important.

blocks.title: For a vertex presentation, determine the occipital position where possible:

blocks.text: Assess the fetal head abdominally using fifths palpable above the pelvic brim.
Locate the fetal back and assess the fetal heart.
“The fetal heart rate is 145 beats per minute and regular.”
If there are concerns about fetal wellbeing, continuous or more frequent fetal monitoring may be required according to the clinical situation.

blocks.title: Perform when clinically indicated and with:

blocks.text: The exact definition can vary according to guideline/framework, but clinically established labour is characterized by:
**Regular painful uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical change.**
From onset of established labour until:
It includes cervical effacement and dilatation.

blocks.text: This will be covered in more detail in the postpartum/third-stage stations.
Cervix remains unchanged over serial examinations.
“I would assess contraction pattern, fetal position and station, maternal and fetal wellbeing, and review the labour progress over time rather than diagnosing arrest from a single examination.”
Full dilatation but fetal head remains high.
Increasing caput with poor descent may indicate:
Mild moulding can occur normally during labour.
Meconium requires appropriate fetal surveillance and management according to the clinical context.
If the fetal heart pattern is abnormal:
**Recognize fetal compromise → call for senior help → initiate appropriate intrapartum assessment/management.**
“The mother is febrile with maternal and fetal tachycardia and uterine tenderness. This raises concern for intra-amniotic infection and requires urgent assessment and management.”

items.text: Cord felt vaginally/seen at the introitus

blocks.text: “I would call for urgent senior assistance, avoid unnecessary handling of the cord, relieve pressure on the presenting part using appropriate positioning/manual elevation as indicated, and prepare for urgent delivery.”
This is not usually diagnosed during the initial examination, but the examiner may ask:
“What emergency could occur immediately after delivery?”

items.text: Failure of the shoulders to deliver after the head

blocks.text: It requires immediate obstetric emergency management.
“I would urgently reassess maternal and fetal wellbeing, contraction pattern, cervical progress, fetal position and station, and obtain senior obstetric review for possible obstructed labour.”

“This is a term woman in established labour. She is clinically well, with stable maternal observations. She has regular contractions occurring four times in 10 minutes, each lasting approximately 50 seconds. The fetus is in a longitudinal lie with cephalic presentation and an occipito-anterior position. The fetal head is well descended. The fetal heart rate is 140 beats per minute and regular. Vaginal examination reveals a soft anterior cervix that is 6 cm dilated and approximately 80% effaced. The membranes are intact and there is no significant caput or moulding.”

“The woman is in active labour with regular contractions occurring every 2–3 minutes, lasting approximately 50–60 seconds. The cervix is 8 cm dilated and approximately 90% effaced. The fetal head is at +1 station with cephalic presentation and an occipito-anterior position. The membranes have ruptured with clear liquor. There is mild caput and no significant moulding. Fetal heart rate is 145 beats per minute.”

“The cervix is fully dilated but the fetal head remains high with poor descent. There is significant caput and moulding. The findings raise concern for obstructed labour/cephalopelvic disproportion. I would urgently reassess maternal and fetal wellbeing and request senior obstetric review.”

“The woman is febrile with maternal tachycardia and uterine tenderness. The liquor is foul-smelling and the fetal heart rate is elevated. These findings raise concern for intra-amniotic infection and require urgent maternal and fetal assessment and treatment.”

content_groups.group_title: Q: How do you know a woman is in established labour?

blocks.text: She has regular painful uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical effacement and dilatation.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What are the three stages of labour?

items.text: First stage — onset of established labour to full cervical dilatation.
Second stage — full cervical dilatation to birth.
Third stage — birth of the baby to delivery of placenta and membranes.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What do you assess during a vaginal examination in labour?

blocks.text: The presenting part is level with the maternal ischial spines.
The presenting part is approximately 2 cm below the ischial spines.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What does severe moulding suggest?

blocks.text: It may indicate difficulty with descent and possible cephalopelvic disproportion or obstructed labour, particularly when associated with other findings.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ Mistake 8 — Calling any prolonged labour “obstructed labour”

blocks.text: Bleeding, fever, meconium, abnormal FHR, poor descent, caput, moulding, cord prolapse.
A very common examiner question is:
**“What would you document after assessing this woman?”**
The strongest candidates don't merely say:

**“She is 6 cm dilated, 80% effaced, with the fetal head at 0 station, occipito-anterior, membranes intact, no significant caput or moulding, with four contractions in ten minutes and a fetal heart rate of 140 bpm. Maternal observations are stable.”**
That gives the examiner a complete picture of **labour + maternal condition + fetal condition + progress**.
